content:
After a long public debate on the so-called Islamic dilemma, the floor was opened and members of the audience lined up with questions. They were short, direct and mostly fair, and they cover most of what a thoughtful Christian or sceptic asks about the Quran and the earlier scriptures: who changed the Bible, why trust a text its prophet did not write, what the Quran means by the Torah, whether a new revelation can reinterpret an old one, and what to make of the Kaaba and the moon-god story.

This article takes nine of those questions in turn. It names no one, quotes no insult and does not rule on who won. For each question it says what the speaker answered, where the site's own articles agree or differ, and which article holds the evidence. Where the speaker's answer was personal, for example on miracles or on how far the hadith reach back, the entry says so, since the site's articles follow the classical method and set out the evidence for it. The related articles are the Islamic dilemma, its Christian twin and revelatory exegesis.

The questioner put it as a puzzle of control. By the seventh century the Gospels had been copied for hundreds of years in many languages and in churches that did not agree with one another, so no one could have altered every copy. The speaker answered that, in the historians' view, the change comes at the start and not later: most of the books are not by the authors the tradition names, so the text has a history from the beginning.

These are two different claims, and the entry keeps them apart. The Quran does not say that every copy was rewritten at one moment. It says that some people "write the 'scripture' with their own hands, then say, 'This is from Allah'" (2:79) and that some "alter the Scripture with their tongues" (3:78).[1] That is about persons and practices, and it does not name a date or a council. The articles on who changed the Bible and the alteration claim before Islam set out what Christians themselves said in the early centuries.

Verdict: the puzzle is fair against a claim of a single act, and the Quran does not make that claim. The question of authorship is a separate matter, and the manuscripts are discussed in the article on transmission.

The speaker agreed that the argument cuts both ways when it is used carelessly, and that a Muslim should not use it against the Gospels without noticing that it applies to his own sources. That is a fair concession, and the site makes it too.

The difference lies in what each tradition claims. The Quran was recited aloud, memorised and written down under the Prophet's eye, and the later copies descend from that recitation, as the article on the Prophet's not writing it down sets out with its sources. The Gospels do not claim to be a dictation from Jesus ﷺ. They are accounts of him by others, and no Christian doctrine needs them to be anything else. The hadith are a third case: their standing rests on chains of narrators, and the article on the isnads says how scholars date them.

The speaker also said that most critical scholars think the Quran goes back to Muhammad ﷺ, and that a historian does not take every hadith as authentic. Verdict: the argument does not defeat either side by itself. What each text claims about its own origin is the point to test.

The questioner cited a report in which the Prophet ﷺ sat on a cushion among a group of Jews, had the Torah brought, put it on the cushion and said he believed in the one who revealed it, and argued that this shows that the Quran's word means the physical text the Jews held. The speaker answered that the word is used for the divine proclamation first and for the written book second, as qurʾān itself names a recitation before it names a book.

The report is real, and it is hard on the speaker's reading, as the questioner said. A fair answer concedes that several Quranic verses speak of a Torah "with" the Jews of Medina (3:93, 5:43), and that the Quran also uses kitāb for a written book. The article on the cushion report sets out its sources and its grading, and the article on kitāb gives the range of the word.

Verdict: both senses are in the Quran. The speaker's answer is right that the word has a wider sense, and the questioner is right that the report points at a book.

A Christian questioner granted for argument that the Quran is true and asked why the same principle does not let the Book of Mormon reinterpret the Quran. The speaker answered that every scriptural religion has this problem and gave the example of the Bahāʾī faith, which treats the Quran as intact and its own scripture as the true interpretation.

The Quran answers the question in its own terms. It names Muhammad ﷺ the seal of the prophets (33:40) and says that the religion is complete (5:3), which closes the door to a later revelation in the Muslim view. The article on the seal weighs the Bahāʾī, Aḥmadī and Mormon readings and shows where the argument works and where it is circular. The point the questioner raised is a real one: a closed canon is a claim, and an outsider cannot test it from inside.

Verdict: the principle is not enough alone. The Muslim case rests on the seal verse and on the Quran's own claim to confirm and watch over what came before. The article on revelatory exegesis says how far that goes.

A long question joined three points. Christians do not say the Old Testament is corrupt. They read it through the New. Verse 10:94 tells the Prophet to "ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you" if he is in doubt, which seems to presuppose a reliable earlier scripture. And how does a reinterpretation reading handle Mark 10:45, "a ransom for many", against the denial in 4:157 that Jesus was killed?[2]

The first two are answered in the article on 10:94, which sets out the verse in context and concedes what it implies. The third is in the article on ransom and the article on the crucifixion. The speaker declined to give a personal reading of Mark 10:45, and said that texts in the New Testament can be read towards a Trinitarian or a Unitarian view. The speaker was asked a related question on John 14:6, "No one comes to the Father, except through me", and answered that for a believer in a true prophet the prophet's reading governs, and that, as far as he remembered, most New Testament scholars doubt that line goes back to Jesus, though he said he would need to check.[3]

Verdict: the questions are real, and the speaker's answers were brief. The evidence on each is in the linked articles.

The speaker's answer on preservation was careful. If "perfectly preserved" means every letter fixed beyond variation, he said, a historian cannot claim it, because there are textual variants; as a believer he treats the text as perfect in another sense. The articles on the seven ahruf, verses read differently and the Uthmanic copies lay out the variants and the reading traditions, and they make the same distinction between differences of reading and differences of text.

The other question asked whether the Quran identifies a prophet such as Elisha clearly enough to be verified without an outside source. The Quran does call itself clear (12:1) and its Arabic clear (26:195), and it names al-Yasaʿ, Elisha, twice (6:86, 38:48).[4] Naming a prophet is not the same as describing his life. The speaker said that interpretation has always disagreed about meanings, and that the claim of clarity is itself debated.

Verdict: the variants are real and are published, and "clear" in the Quran describes its language and its message and not every detail. A reader who wants the details has always gone to the commentaries.

The speaker said that by "secular" he meant a method, a historical-critical one, and not the scholar's belief: plenty of the best scholars of the Bible are Christians, and what he wanted to avoid was an apologist's reading made to fit a later orthodoxy.

The site agrees about the method. The Faruqian principle behind it is to turn "confrontation and reciprocal condemnations" into "a scholarly investigation of the genesis and development of the religions", so as to separate historical accretions from the given of revelation.[5] The article on Western scholars of Islam and the article on the scholars who shaped Islamic study list those whose work is used, Muslim and non-Muslim, and say where each is weak.

Verdict: the label does not matter, and the method does. A believer who follows evidence and a sceptic who follows evidence should reach the same facts, and may differ on what the facts mean.

The speaker called the moon-god theory a polemic with no historical basis, and said that recent work shows the pagans of Mecca moving towards a single high God and using astral and other beings as intermediaries. The claim appeared in a 1994 pamphlet and a 2001 book by an American Christian apologist, and Muslim and non-Muslim writers have replied to it in print; an academic quoted in a reference article on the theory calls it an insult to Arab Christians who use the name Allah for God.[6] Arabic-speaking Christians do use the word.

The second half of the question is a fair one. The Kaaba, the pilgrimage and the sacred months existed before Islam, and the Quran refers to pre-Islamic worship in many verses. The article on rites before Islam and the article on the Black Stone grant what is known and say what the Quran changed. A reference to an earlier practice is not the same as copying it, and the Quran's own claim is that these rites go back to Abraham.

Verdict: the moon-god story has no support in the evidence cited, and the pre-Islamic background is real and acknowledged. The two should not be confused.

This was put to the other debater, and the speaker asked for a short reply. The Christian answer was that the new covenant explains fulfilment and is not a patch. The speaker's reply was that the Quran too speaks of a covenant with the believers.

Both sides can point to texts. The prophet Jeremiah says that God will "make a new covenant with the house of Israel", one in which the law is put "in their inward parts", and Hebrews says that "in that he says, 'A new covenant', he has made the first old".[7] The Quran has covenants of its own: God took the covenant of the prophets (3:81, 33:7), bound the believers by a covenant (5:7), and took a covenant from the Children of Israel (5:12).[8]

These are not the same idea. In the Christian reading the older covenant is made obsolete. In the Quran the earlier covenants are confirmed and brought to a conclusion by one messenger, as the article on the covenant of the prophets sets out. Verdict: the comparison is fair as a question of method, and the content differs. A covenant that replaces and a covenant that confirms are not one thing.

The bottom line

The nine questions have answers, and several of them were made fairer by the speaker's own concessions: the argument from the Prophet's not writing cuts both ways, the Torah of the Quran has two senses, and the variants in the text of the Quran are real. The answers where the speaker's view differs from the site's are on miracles, on how far the hadith reach, and on the status of the Quran's perfection, and in each the site follows the classical method and gives the evidence for it.

The moon-god theory and the claim of a single act of corruption have the weakest support, and the questions about a closed canon and about covenants are the ones that remain open between the two sides. A reader is entitled to weigh them. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:79 and 3:78, Saheeh International translation, read on the Quran.com API.
  2. Mark 10:45 and Quran 4:157 and 10:94, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com) and on the Quran.com API.
  3. John 14:6, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com). The speaker's answers are summarised from the transcript of the debate's question session, which is a speech transcript and was not checked against the video.
  4. Quran 12:1, 26:195, 6:86 and 38:48, Saheeh International.
  5. Al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life (International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2nd edition, 1992), chapter 4, section IV, as set out in the project's Faruqian core document; the quotation comes from that document's transcription of the book's text layer and was not rechecked on the printed page.
  6. The claim of the moon-god theory and the replies to it, as summarised in the English Wikipedia article "Allah as a lunar deity" and in the reply published by Islamic Awareness (a Muslim apologetics site, so partisan), read through a web search for this article; the sources were not opened in full, and the quotation attributed to an academic is as given in the Wikipedia article. That Arabic-speaking Christians use the name Allah for God is stated from general knowledge.
  7. Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Hebrews 8:13, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  8. Quran 3:81, 33:7, 5:7 and 5:12, Saheeh International.
